**Text Two: *****Young and dyslexic? You’ve got it going on***

Remind yourself of the extract Young and dyslexic? You’ve got it going on (Text Two as found in the [*June 2023 R exam paper*](https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International-GCSE/English-Language-A/2016/Exam-materials/4ea1-01r-que-20230606.pdf)).

How does the writer, Benjamin Zephaniah, use language and structure in **Text Two** to convey his experiences?

You should support your answer with close reference to the extract, including **brief** quotations.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer The writer, Benjamin Zephaniah, uses a range of language and structural devices to convey both his negative and positive experiences of education, presenting his journey from struggle to success. He ultimately encourages others to feel empowered by their differences. Firstly, Zephaniah opens with the blunt statement “As a child I suffered,” immediately setting a serious and emotive tone. The use of the verb “suffered” highlights the extent of his early difficulties, which is then juxtaposed with a tone of hope by using the contrasting conjunction “but” to mark a turning point as he “learned to turn dyslexia” to his advantage and to see the world “more creatively”. He uses a cyclical structure, as the phrase “We are the architects. We are the designers,” is repeated both at the beginning and end of the text, reinforcing his message of creativity and pride and creating an uplifting and positive tone. Within this paragraph, he also moves from the first person singular “I” to the more inclusive first person plural “we” to convey the fact that he is part of a wider community of people with dyslexia, something which he appears to be proud of. Zephaniah also uses anecdotes to convey his experiences, especially the negative ones. He recalls being told to “shut up, stupid boy” and being called “stupid” for thinking creatively. He also recounts his experiences of being stereotyped through being told that he would simply “end up being a good sportsperson”. Although he didn’t realise that he was being stereotyped at the time, he uses the example to highlight how people with dyslexia were often underestimated, which is something he challenges throughout the text. Furthermore, the writer structures the text using a chronological timeline, using time markers such as “when I was 10 or 11” and “when I was 13”. This allows the reader to follow Zephaniah’s development over time, mirroring the growth in his own confidence and self-acceptance, and to establish the fact that he has overcome the challenges he faced. Towards the end of the text, Zephaniah adopts a more advisory tone, addressing the reader directly by saying “if you’re dyslexic” to offer reassurance and encouragement. His confident and self-assured tone continues to the end, advising those reading that “it’s not you”. He does not convey anger at the negative experiences he has had, but rather chooses to focus on his success and gives advice to parents through the imperative “don’t think of it as a defect” to reinforce his positive and hopeful message. > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a well-developed and perceptive response that fully meets the criteria for Level 5. **Question 5 is based on both Text One and Text Two as found in the **[*June 2023 R exam paper*](https://qualifications.pearson.com/content/dam/pdf/International-GCSE/English-Language-A/2016/Exam-materials/4ea1-01r-que-20230606.pdf)**.**

Compare how the writers present their ideas and perspectives about the experiences described.

Support your answer with detailed examples from both texts, including **brief** quotations.
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer While both texts are about British men overcoming dyslexia and achieving success, Carter in Text One succeeded despite his dyslexia, whereas Zephaniah in Text Two feels he succeeded because of it. As young boys, both men seem to have had quite a difficult time. In Text One, some teachers suggested that Will Carter would end up “a criminal” and the writer states that he had been “miserable and lonely at primary school”. The writer uses the blunt, short statement “school was torment” to underscore what an unhappy and distressing time it was for Carter. Similarly, despite being written in the first person rather than the third person narrative used in Text One, Zephaniah conveys the difficulties he experienced in his early years through the equally blunt “as a child I suffered”. In addition, in both texts the men had teachers who were not interested in hearing their opinions. In Text One, Carter’s teacher asks him if he was a “retard” and asks him to read out loud as a “way of silencing” him because she knew he couldn’t. In Text Two, Zephaniah was told to “shut up, stupid boy” and he reports that he was called “stupid for even thinking about it”. Both men were wrongly considered to have low levels of intelligence by ignorant teachers who spoke to them in a shocking and disrespectful way. Both were devalued and stereotyped by these teachers, with some thinking that Carter would end up a “criminal” and Zephaniah being told that he would “end up being a good sportsperson” because “we can’t all be intelligent”. The use of the direct speech in both texts emphasises the impact these teachers and what they said had on both men, shaping their views of themselves and their ability to succeed. There is also a difference in the men’s experiences due when they were at school. In Text One we are told that Carter at age 13, knowing he had dyslexia, went to his teacher to “demand a teaching assistant and a laptop”. In contrast, Zephaniah did not even know what dyslexia was until he was 21 and his lack of understanding is conveyed through the question “Do I need an operation?”. The purpose of Text One is to inform readers about the tough challenges people with dyslexia face via Will Carter’s story, in which he and his grandparents had to fight and demonstrate that he was being discriminated against. He was able to use the assistance of technology which, for him, “changed everything”, but the tone is still cautionary as Carter believes the education sector has still been “too slow to embrace” all of the technology available. Carter believes he has been lucky to get the support he required and not everyone is so fortunate. In contrast, technology and additional support were not available to Zephaniah and yet his message and tone are more positive overall. Zephaniah believes that dyslexia can help creativity and urges people to “use it to your advantage”, using his own success as an example. Text Two employs a more light-hearted, celebratory and reassuring tone, ending with the inclusive “us dyslexic people, we’ve got it going on” whereas Text One ends on a more downbeat note. > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a well-developed and perceptive response that fully meets the criteria for Level 5. It opens with a confident thesis statement and goes on to consider a varied and comprehensive range of comparisons between the texts, exploring and analysing the writers’ choices to convey their ideas and experiences. > > | **AO3**: Explore links and connections between writers’ ideas and perspectives, as well as how these are conveyed:

- You have analysed the writers’ ideas and perspectives, including how theme, language and/or structure are used, across both texts

- Your use of references from both texts fully support the points being made | > |---|---| > **[exam-tip]** > - Start with a thesis statement that makes a point of comparison > - Try to ensure you deal with each extract equally and that your references are balanced across both texts > - Ensure you allow enough time to tackle this question properly, as it is worth nearly half of the marks for reading

parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer The writer, Emma Levine, uses a wide range of language and structural techniques to create an atmosphere filled with excitement and danger, as she recounts the experience of watching a high-stakes donkey race in Pakistan. From the start, Levine builds excitement through her description of the build-up to the race. She describes how the lads were “suddenly fired up with enthusiasm” and the metaphor “fired up” conveys a sudden burst of energy and eagerness. This is reinforced structurally through the use of direct speech, such as “point your camera towards the race” which creates a sense of urgency and immediacy, suggesting that this will potentially be a dangerous spectacle which will be worth recording. The element of danger is further introduced through her description of the chaotic and uncontrolled nature of the race. Levine writes that “This was Formula One without rules” using a powerful comparison to a famously fast and dangerous sport to emphasise the complete lack of safety. The tricolon, “without rules…anarchic and a complete flouting of every type of traffic rule”, lists escalating dangers to highlight how the scene was unpredictable and perilous. Structurally, the long sentence reflects the overwhelming and breathless nature of the scene, mirroring Levine’s own frantic observations. The writer also uses sound to create a vivid and sensory atmosphere. The phrase “horns tooting, bells ringing, and the special rattles used just for this purpose” includes a list of noises that builds a loud and chaotic soundscape, showing how the race assaults the senses. The repetition of onomatopoeia and listing enhances the excitement while also suggesting confusion and disarray. Later in the text, the mood shifts dramatically as the race ends and conflict erupts. Levine uses short, punchy sentences such as “And then the trouble began” which immediately signals a change in tone and creates suspense. This is followed by the tricolon “Voices were raised, fists were out and tempers rising” which combines rising tension with a suggestion of physical danger. The repetition of “and” increases the pace, mirroring the way the events seem to spiral out of control. Finally, the danger becomes more personal when Levine reveals that Yaqoob and Iqbal “were nervous” and that the situation was “starting to get nasty”. These quotes show that even those who were previously excited are now wary, creating a sense of menace. Structurally, this moment is placed near the end to serve as a climax to the rising tension throughout the piece, emphasising how quickly excitement can turn into threat. Overall, Levine skilfully uses both language and structure to build a vivid account of a thrilling but dangerous event, keeping the reader engaged and alert to the unpredictable nature of the race. > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a well-developed and detailed analysis of both language and structure, maintaining a clear focus on the question. **Question 5 is based on both Text One and Text Two as found in the **[*January 2023 R exam paper*](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/03/4ea1-01r-que-20230113.pdf).

Compare how the writers present their ideas and perspectives about their experiences.

Support your answer with detailed examples from both texts, including **brief** quotations.

**[22 marks]**
parts.solutionMd:
## Model answer While both texts describe exciting moments in unfamiliar cultural settings, Michael Palin in Himalaya presents his experience with humour and fascination, while Emma Levine in A Game of Polo with a Headless Goat portrays hers with excitement and a touch of chaos. Both writers reveal the unpredictability of the events they witness, but their tones and perspectives differ. Firstly, while both extracts are first hand accounts by writers who are involved in filming a race while travelling, both writers use differing tones to shape how they present their experiences to the reader. In Himalaya, Palin’s tone is light-hearted and self-aware as he describes watching a bull race in Pakistan with Prince Malik. His perspective is one of curious amusement, observing the traditions without claiming to fully understand them, as he muses that “there’s clearly no point in arguing” and that it “doesn’t seem to matter that no one really knows what they’re doing.” In contrast, in A Game of Polo with a Headless Goat, Levine’s tone is energetic and lively. She builds tension by describing how they waited, thinking that the “race had been cancelled,” before the donkey race exploded into action, with “vehicles roaring up in their wake” before continuing to evoke the frenzy and chaos of the race itself. Both writers “set the scene” before the race. In Palin’s account, we are introduced to Prince Malik the day before the race, and in Levine’s text she describes the extended anticipation as she waits for the racers. In addition, both writers experience and describe scenes of mayhem. In Text One, Palin describes how one of the team of bulls “plunge headfirst into the crowd” and “two more hurtle off towards a flagpole, taking out the flag”. In Text Two, Levine compares the donkey race to a “city-centre rush hour gone anarchic”, and both writers reference the uproar created by these unusual races. The people involved in both of these events seem to be in precarious positions, as in Palin’s account a rider “stands, as best he can, on…a glorified tin-lid” and in Text Two they are “perched on top of the tiny carts”. Both writers therefore seem bemused and a little confused by what they are experiencing. Levine’s use of dialogue creates a sense of intimacy, whereas Palin’s observations seem more detached. Furthermore, both writers also reflect on the risks involved for the people taking part, whilst having a rather casual attitude towards the wellbeing of the animals themselves. Palin acknowledges the danger lightly, describing how Prince Malik’s driver had a reputation for reckless driving, but his tone stays humorous. However, he also states that the bulls are “dragged unceremoniously to the starting line” and does not make any further comment about their treatment, other than remarking that some seem intent on reaching the “freedom of the fresh-cut wheat fields beyond.” Levine’s account feels more tense and dangerous as it progresses, as she describes the speeding cars and the unpredictable donkeys. She notes that the jockeys are “using their whips energetically, although not cruelly” and noting that the “leading donkey swerved, lost his footing” and crashed. Both highlight the daring nature of the events they witness, but Palin’s humour contrasts with Levine’s more breathless excitement. In conclusion, both Himalaya and A Game of Polo with a Headless Goat explore the thrill and unpredictability of cultural traditions, but they differ in tone and perspective. Palin offers a humorous, observational account, while Levine plunges the reader into the wild, chaotic energy of the race. Together, they show how different writers can capture similar experiences in contrasting ways, using tone, structure, and language to shape their perspectives. > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a well-developed and perceptive response that fully meets the criteria for Level 5. Both texts highlight the ignorance and cruelty surrounding dyslexia in the past. Wigan is “ridiculed by teachers and peers alike”, while Zephaniah explains that his generation experienced “no compassion, no understanding and no humanity” within the education system. Each writer also reveals how dyslexic children were underestimated and stereotyped. Yaqoob’s daring nature is demonstrated when he “revved up the engine” to join the convoy, and the writer admires his skill, explaining that he “chose exactly the right moment” to move into the race. Athletes, for instance, often embody resilience and dedication, while certain public figures use their platforms to advocate for meaningful causes. Likewise, Sir David Attenborough has long utilised his global reach to raise awareness about environmental issues with integrity. When young people idolise those who prioritise wealth, image, or notoriety over compassion and responsibility, the consequences can be harmful. Fame, after all, is not a virtue; it is merely a status. Moreover, the crafted nature of celebrity life can create dangerous illusions. Their lives may appear glamorous and effortless, but these portrayals often lack authenticity. For impressionable audiences, this can foster insecurity, unrealistic aspirations and a distorted sense of success. It is worth asking, then: who makes a genuinely valuable role model? The adolescent years are complex, unpredictable and emotionally charged. Who among us haven’t been subjected to eye-rolls, sighing and mumbling as our offspring emerge at some time in the early afternoon from their pits? It is a time defined by the search for identity, independence and acceptance. As the teenage brain continues to mature, it is not surprising that teenagers may appear erratic, withdrawn, or experience unexplainable outbursts. Teenage development is frequently influenced by external pressures. The demands of academic success, the complexities of peer relationships and the often unrealistic portrayals on social media all contribute to mounting stress. Concerns surrounding body image, the desire to conform, or the need to stand out can lead to fluctuating self-esteem: confidence one moment, uncertainty the next. The result is a uniquely turbulent stage of life, where guidance, patience, and understanding are not simply helpful but essential. **Common Challenges Teenagers May Face** Teenagers today can face a variety of issues. Anxiety and depression are increasingly common, and this can be made worse by peer pressure; fitting in can be difficult if you are not sure where exactly you fit! In addition, the pressure to achieve at school or college can lead to burnout or feelings of not being good enough. This can take its toll on teenagers’ self-esteem, which can have implications well into adulthood. **How Parents and Carers Can Offer Support** 1. **Listen Without Judgement** Create a safe space where your teenager feels heard. Avoid jumping to conclusions or offering immediate solutions. Sometimes, they need understanding more than advice. 2. **Maintain Open and Honest Communication** Be transparent about your own experiences when appropriate. ### Model answer **The Key to Success: The Power of Preparation** When people say, “The key to success is being prepared”, they are absolutely right. Preparation means taking the time to get ready for what lies ahead. It involves planning, practising, organising, and gathering the information, skills or tools needed to face any challenge with confidence. Whether you are sitting an exam, playing a sports match, attending a job interview, or delivering an important speech, being prepared makes all the difference. **Reducing stress and building confidence** One of the most important reasons why preparation leads to success is that it helps to reduce anxiety. When you know you have done everything possible to get ready, you feel much calmer and more in control. For example, if you have studied thoroughly for an exam by revising regularly, creating revision notes, and practising past papers, you will walk into the exam hall feeling focused and confident. On the other hand, leaving everything to the last minute can lead to stress, panic, and poor performance. Therefore, ensuring that you have prepared thoroughly will lead to better outcomes. **Handling the unexpected** Preparation also allows you to deal with unexpected problems more effectively. Life rarely goes exactly according to plan, but being prepared helps you to adapt. A footballer who has trained hard can still perform well even if the weather changes or the opposing team is stronger than expected. Similarly, a student who has revised a wide range of topics will be able to answer tricky exam questions, even if they are different from what they expected. While it is impossible to prepare for every possible situation or scenario, it is possible to reduce the chance of unexpected surprises by preparing properly. **Spotting weaknesses early** Another benefit of preparation is that it gives you time to spot any weaknesses. When you begin preparing, you might realise that there are areas you don’t fully understand or skills you need to practise further. This allows you to correct mistakes before they become serious problems. For example, someone preparing for a public speaking competition may discover that they speak too quickly or lose track of their main points. Through practice, they can work on their delivery, making their speech clearer and more effective. This is why it is so important to prepare and practise for big things like exams; knowing what you need to work on in advance means that you can concentrate more on revising those areas. **Developing life skills** Preparation also teaches valuable life skills such as discipline, organisation, and time management. Learning how to break tasks down into smaller steps and stick to a plan helps to avoid last-minute panic. People who prepare regularly often become more efficient and productive, which benefits them in school, work, and personal life. **Long-term success** Finally, preparation builds confidence because it shows you have put in the effort beforehand. This confidence allows you to perform at your best, even under pressure. Successful athletes, musicians, and professionals all understand that preparation is what allows them to deliver excellent results when it matters most. In conclusion, being prepared is one of the most important steps towards success in any area of life. It reduces stress, helps you handle challenges, highlights areas for improvement, and builds lifelong skills.
